label: 0058 · Smoothed in time, 1997–2025 (one QP over 53 windows): 0054 with the Tohoku University seafloor GNSS-A network's frame velocity estimated, tied to the co-located Japan Coast Guard site, uncorrelated noise, background coupling from −1 to 1, fourteen slow slip events as signal, fixed 747-site network, UNR positions (MAP)
description: 0054 with one change in how the seafloor data enter. Tohoku University's GNSS-A series (G01–G20) are published without a stated reference frame. 0052–0057 convert them as North-America-fixed and hold that conversion exactly. Here the Tohoku University network gets a velocity offset of its own, one east and one north rate for all its sites, with a prior from the one close pair of Tohoku University and Japan Coast Guard sites (G14 and MYGI, 25 km apart): (−12.5, 0) ± 5 mm/yr. The estimate is (−14.5, +2.3) mm/yr, 0.4 sd from that tie. The Japan Coast Guard sites (ITRF2020) and the onshore data keep their frames. In the onshore frame the model now moves the Tohoku University sites 6–19 mm/yr less landward than 0054 does (13 mm/yr on average), and the offset takes up the difference: their residuals are 47.6 mm against 48.4, while the model at the Japan Coast Guard sites moves by less than 3 mm/yr. Coupling off Miyagi at 0–20 km in 2012–2021 is 1.31 (0054: 1.37), held there by the Japan Coast Guard sites MYGI and KAMS. North and south of Miyagi, off Iwate, Fukushima and Ibaraki, shallow coupling is 0.09–0.15 lower. The onshore fit is unchanged. Held-out seafloor sites are predicted better than by 0054 (cross-validation +1,270 against +1,138, all of the gain at Tohoku University sites), and held-out onshore windows as well (+532 against +548). The seafloor arrows show the model in the onshore frame, without the offset. Two more fields split the Japan Trench coupling. Where the coupling along the plate motion exceeds 1, the excess is drawn as the slab's excess velocity (mm/yr) and the rest as coupling to the slab (at most 1). A slab segment moving landward faster than the Pacific plate beneath an interface locked to it, as relaxation of the mantle beneath the slab would drive it, gives exactly the surface velocities of that excess coupling, whatever the depth of the shear zone beneath the slab. Off Miyagi at 0–20 km the excess averages 95 mm/yr in 2012–2014, 54 in 2014–2016, 33 in 2016–2019 and 19 in 2019–2025 (plate rate 84 mm/yr), so the interface itself never slips in the normal sense. Seafloor data: Japan Coast Guard (CC BY-NC 4.0) and Tohoku University (CC BY 4.0).
